lesson.title: Selective Repeat: Only Resend What Actually Went Missing
lesson.summary: Selective Repeat ARQ improves on go back N by letting the receiver buffer out of order frames and acknowledge them individually, so the sender only needs to retransmit the specific frame that was lost or corrupted rather than an entire run of already good data.
lesson.body:
Selective repeat starts from the same sliding window foundation as go back N but makes a different tradeoff at the receiver. Instead of a receive window of size 1 that rejects anything out of order, selective repeat gives the receiver a window as wide as the sender's, letting it accept and buffer frames that arrive ahead of the one it is currently waiting for. The receiver acknowledges each frame individually as it arrives, correct or not, rather than only issuing cumulative acknowledgments for a contiguous run. This means a single lost frame no longer poisons everything sent after it.

Trace the same scenario used for go back N so the contrast is direct. Window size 4, sequence numbers 0 through 7, sender transmits frames 0, 1, 2, and 3. Frame 0 arrives fine, receiver sends ACK0. Frame 1 is corrupted and discarded, with no ACK1 sent. Frames 2 and 3 arrive undamaged. Under selective repeat, the receiver does not discard them: it buffers frame 2 and frame 3 and sends ACK2 and ACK3 individually, even though frame 1 is still missing. When the sender's timer for frame 1 expires, it retransmits only frame 1. Once frame 1 arrives, the receiver now has 1, 2, and 3 all in hand, delivers all three in order up to the application, and slides its window forward. Frames 2 and 3 never had to be resent.

That efficiency is not free. The receiver needs buffer space for up to N out of order frames, along with logic to reassemble them into the correct sequence before handing data to the layer above, and the sender needs to track and time each outstanding frame individually rather than treating the whole window as one block. This is meaningfully more bookkeeping on both ends than go back N requires, which is exactly the tradeoff: selective repeat spends memory and per frame timers to save retransmission bandwidth, while go back N spends retransmission bandwidth to save memory and complexity.

Selective repeat has a subtler correctness requirement than go back N does. Because both the sender's window and the receiver's window can independently hold up to N frames, the sequence number space must be at least twice the window size, N less than or equal to M divided by 2, where M is the number of distinct sequence numbers. If the window were allowed to be larger relative to M, an old, already delivered frame retransmitted after a very delayed acknowledgment could carry the same sequence number as a genuinely new frame currently sitting in the receiver's window, and the receiver would have no way to tell them apart. This constraint is stricter than go back N's because selective repeat's receiver window overlaps in sequence number space with frames the sender might still resend.

In practice, selective repeat's approach, or a close variant of it, shows up wherever the cost of retransmitting is high relative to buffering, such as TCP's selective acknowledgment option layered on top of its own cumulative acknowledgment base, which lets a TCP receiver tell the sender exactly which out of order segments it already has so the sender does not blindly resend an entire window's worth of data after only one segment is lost.
